It is the sole living representative of its family (Ornithorhynchidae) and genus (Ornithorhynchus), though a number of related species appear in the fossil record.\n\nThe bizarre appearance of the platypus—with its duck-like bill, beaver-like tail, and otter-like feet—made it the subject of much curiosity when it was first encountered by European naturalists in 1798. The unusual features of the platypus, including its venomous spurs, electroreception, and ability to lay eggs, have made it an important subject in the study of evolutionary biology.\n\nThe platypus is an excellent swimmer and spends much of its time in the water. The platypus uses its bill to detect the electrical signals generated by the muscles of its prey, a unique ability among mammals.\n\nThe platypus is a solitary animal and is most active during the night. It is the sole living representative of its family (Ornithorhynchidae) and genus (Ornithorhynchus), though a number of related species appear in the fossil record.\n\nThe bizarre appearance of the platypus—with its duck-like bill, beaver-like tail, and otter-like feet—made it the subject of much curiosity when it was first encountered by European naturalists in 1798.
